questions.question: In letter-shift coding, if CAT is coded as DBU, what rule is being applied?
options: Each letter is shifted forward by 1 position
Each letter is replaced by its mirror letter
Each letter is replaced by a number
questions.rationale: C->D, A->B, T->U — each letter moves forward exactly one position in the alphabet, a uniform +1 shift.

questions.question: What happens when a letter-shift rule pushes a letter past Z (e.g., Y + 3)?
options: It wraps around to the start of the alphabet (A, B, C...)
It becomes a number instead of a letter
The question has no valid answer
questions.rationale: The alphabet is treated as a loop of 26 letters, so shifting past Z wraps around back to A, then B, and so on.

questions.question: In substitution/mirror coding where A<->Z, B<->Y, C<->X and so on, what is true about each mapped pair's positions?
questions.rationale: Mirror coding reflects each letter's position around the alphabet's center, so a letter at position p maps to position 27-p, meaning every mapped pair sums to 27.

questions.question: Why is it important to verify a coding rule against every letter of the given example, not just the first one or two?
options: It isn't important — the first letter is always enough
Some questions apply a non-uniform rule, or an exception on one letter, that only shows up later in the word
Longer words always use number coding instead
It only matters for reverse coding
questions.rationale: Some coding questions mix a shift with an exception on a specific letter (often the last or a repeated one) — checking only the first letters can lead to applying the wrong rule to the new word.
